item.title: Exploring our diplomatic ties
item.description:
We are encouraged by the recent diplomatic engagements exploring a potential free trade agreement (FTA) between Bangladesh and Uzbekistan.
Bangladesh’s economic diplomacy has long remained narrowly tethered to a handful of traditional Western and regional markets, leaving our export basket and strategic partnerships overly vulnerable to external shocks.
To that end, ties with nations such as Uzbekistan signal a refreshing and long-overdue evolution in our foreign policy.
Reaching beyond our usual comfort zones to forge robust trade and investment corridors is, at this point, the logical and sensible approach.
As Bangladesh navigates arguably its most challenging economic period in its five and a half decades of being a sovereign state, with slowing domestic growth and mounting global trade pressures, diversifying our international partnerships must become a central pillar of statecraft.
Central Asia offers untapped potential, rich resources, and expanding consumer markets that can absorb our manufactured goods, particularly ready-made garments, while opening new channels for agricultural, technological, and infrastructural collaboration.
Establishing direct connectivity, streamlining business-to-business contacts, and pursuing bilateral FTAs with nations outside our traditional orbit will not only provide much-needed resilience to our external sector but also offer genuine space for further growth and potential innovation.
However, high-level diplomatic handshakes and exploratory talks must quickly translate into concrete action. Historically, our trade ambitions have often stalled in bureaucratic hesitation, failing to move past preliminary memorandums.
The government must therefore aggressively follow through on these emerging ties, and beyond our positive talks with Uzbekistan, continue to explore strengthening ties with other non-traditional partners across the globe.
Diversifying our trade geography, reducing reliance on saturated markets, and actively pursuing economic diplomacy should, over time, lead to long-term prosperity. It is time for us to continue casting a wider net on the global stage.

item.title: Helping teachers keep up
item.description:
It goes without saying that in an era where students navigate complex digital landscapes with ease, educators can no longer rely on chalkboard methods of the past.
To that end, we agree with Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon’s recent call for teachers to master technology and artificial intelligence (AI) to keep pace with digitally fluent students.
To maintain academic relevance, our teaching corps must indeed embrace technological innovation, critical research, and inclusive classroom practices. All of that is a given, and difficult to argue against.
However, telling teachers to adapt without giving them the tools to do so is an exercise in futility. That, unfortunately, has been the reality for some time now when it comes to our education.
Ambitious directives that have been handed down from administrative boardrooms are meaningless if the ground-level reality of our schools and education institutions remains woefully underfunded and disregarded.
Instructors - particularly in rural and under-resourced institutions - grapple with chronic shortages of basic digital infrastructure, inadequate computer labs, unreliable internet, and zero structured training modules.
Expecting such educators to independently bridge the digital divide while burdened by heavy workloads and administrative neglect is completely unrealistic and shows a lack of awareness on the part of the authorities regarding the reality of such educators.
If the government is serious about modernizing our education system, rhetoric must be matched with substantial state investment. Meaningful digital transformation will require comprehensive, continuous, and well-funded professional development programs that equip every teacher with hands-on AI and technology training.
Educators must embrace the challenge of lifelong learning, but the state must provide the robust institutional backing, resources, and institutional support required to make that growth possible.
We cannot build a future-ready education system by demanding modern outcomes from neglected, unsupported teachers.

item.title: The death of browsing
item.description:
There was a time when retail therapy lived up to its name.
Walking into a store, whether a neighbourhood superstore or a trendy lifestyle outlet like Shwapno or Miniso, offered a quiet escape.
A shopper could drift along the aisles, pause to inspect an unfamiliar gadget, read product labels, or simply indulge in the mindless joy of browsing.
It was an unhurried, low-pressure experience where decision-making happened at the consumer’s own pace.
Today, that tranquil space has been replaced by a subtle, relentless tension.
The moment you step through the entrance of a modern retail outlet, you are greeted not with subtle hospitality, but with a sharp, chorus-like shout of "Welcome!" designed less to make you feel comfortable and more to signal that you are now under active surveillance.
From that second onward, the modern retail experience becomes an exercise in evasion.
Staff members shadow your every movement. "What are you looking for, ma'am?" "Have you tried this new lotion?" "We have a promotion on this item today."
What line management calls "proactive customer assistance" feels almost like continuous harassment.
Instead of creating an environment conducive to organic discovery, this aggressive push marketing destroys the mental space needed to make buying decisions -- and ultimately hurts the merchant’s bottom line.
Retail operations often operate on a flawed metric: Equating floor staff proximity with superior customer service.
Management training modules frequently mandate that employees approach every customer within seconds of entry, pitch active promotions, and remain within arm’s reach to offer continuous assistance.
In business theory, this is intended to maximize basket size, prevent shoplifting, and project attentiveness.
In practice, however, it fundamentally misunderstands consumer psychology.
Modern retail thrives on passive browsing -- the psychological phenomenon where a customer enters a shop with no specific intent to buy, but leaves with a basket full of unneeded items simply because they were allowed the time and mental peace to admire them.
When a sales associate physically shadows a shopper, the consumer's cognitive load spikes.
The brain shifts from a state of open curiosity to defense.
You can no longer look at an aesthetic desk lamp or an interesting cosmetic product and wonder how it fits into your life; your mental bandwidth is entirely consumed by formulating polite ways to decline unwanted sales pitches or plotting an exit strategy from the aisle.
The immediate result of this invasive hovering is "cart abandonment" -- not on a website, but in real life.
Consider a typical visit to a grocery chain’s frozen food aisle: A shopper enters looking for chicken salami.
Finding the shelf empty, they are immediately cornered by a promoter persistently pushing frozen parathas.
Despite multiple polite refusals, the sales pitch continues unabated. Overwhelmed and irritated, the shopper flees the section entirely to escape the social pressure.
It is only after returning home that they realize they could have easily substituted the salami with chicken sausages -- a cross-sell opportunity completely destroyed by overzealous push tactics.
The cost of short-term conversions
Why do retail businesses double down on tactics that alienate their customer base? The answer lies in misaligned key performance indicators (KPIs).
On paper, push marketing generates measurable short-term wins.
An aggressive floor associate can occasionally pressure an indecisive customer into buying a featured product just to end the uncomfortable interaction.
In daily sales reports, this looks like a successful conversion attributable to staff initiative.
What management fails to track, however, are the long-term losses:
In an era where e-commerce offers friction-free, silent shopping from the comfort of one's couch, physical brick-and-mortar stores have precisely one major advantage: Tactile experience and environment .
When stores ruin that environment with noise and physical boundary-crossing, they hand their entire market share directly to online platforms.
Redefining in-store engagement
Fixing the retail environment does not require abandoning customer support altogether; it requires transitioning from push assistance to permission-based service.
Retail leaders aiming to rebuild customer loyalty and maximize true retention can consider several structural remedies:
Customer service was never meant to be an exercise in coercion.
At its core, good retail service is about removing friction, not creating it.
When businesses mistake constant interruption for dedication, they trade sustainable customer retention for short-sighted sales pushes.
The modern consumer does not want to be chased down an aisle or pressured into buying frozen bread when they come for cold cuts.
They want the freedom to browse, evaluate, and enjoy the physical space at their own pace.
Until retail operations learn to respect the quiet psychology of shopping, their floor staff will continue to drive away the very customers they are paid to welcome.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Building workplaces free from sexual harassment
item.description:
Bangladesh has taken important steps on sexual harassment at work. The Labour Act addresses aspects of the issue, and Bangladesh has ratified ILO Convention No 190 (C190) on Violence and Harassment. With the Labour rules under review, the challenge is to turn legal commitments into a coherent system that workers can trust, organisations can implement and regulators can enforce.
This is first a matter of rights. No one should have to trade dignity or safety for work. C190 recognizes the right to a world of work free from violence and harassment and calls for prevention, protection, enforcement, and remedies.
It is also a productivity issue. The International Labour Organization reports that workplace sexual harassment cost the world $2.6 billion in lost productivity in 2018, alongside $0.9bn in other financial costs.
Unsafe workplaces contribute to absenteeism, turnover, and disengagement; poorly handled complaints can escalate into disputes and reputational damage. Prevention and effective response are not simply compliance costs; they are part of good governance and risk management. The business case reinforces the rights-based case; it does not replace it.
The development sector has an equal stake. Donors expect credible protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (PSEAH) systems: Safe reporting, competent investigations, non-retaliation, and support.
For the government, this means giving effect to Bangladesh’s international commitments. Bangladesh ratified C190 on 20 November 2025; it enters into force for Bangladesh on 20 November 2026. Its gender-responsive approach spans prevention, enforcement, remedies, investigation, training, and social dialogue. The rules reform is an opportunity to make these principles workable.
What needs to happen next?
The aim should be a coherent system, not more requirements for their own sake.
First , clarify the relationship between Sections 23, 24, 332, and 332A. Sections 23 and 24 provide the misconduct and disciplinary framework, while Sections 332 and 332A address prevention and the complaints committee.
The law should clarify how complaints and investigations connect with disciplinary proceedings: Who investigates, who decides, what safeguards apply, and how remedies follow.
Investigators should establish findings on the evidence; the appropriate authority should decide on action in accordance with law and due process. The committee need not replace disciplinary authority, but the pathway from complaint to decision and remedy must be clear. If the Act does not support it, amendment may be needed.
Second , operationalize Section 332. The rules should translate employers’ preventive duties into practical expectations on policies, risk assessment, training, reporting channels and protection from retaliation.
Third , give Section 332A clear procedures. The Act provides for a five-member complaints committee, with a majority of women, a woman chair and two members from organizations working on gender and sexual violence. The rules should clarify its mandate, independence, timelines, confidentiality, reporting lines, and safeguards against interference.
Fourth , establish an end-to-end process for receiving concerns, assessing safety, selecting an investigator, managing conflicts of interest, assessing evidence, deciding on action, informing parties, and providing remedies. It should address harassment involving supervisors, contractors, clients, and service providers.
Fifth , protect complainants, witnesses, and committee members against retaliation while balancing confidentiality with the respondent’s right to know and respond. An allegation that cannot be established is not, for that reason alone, malicious.
Finally , make the rules workable for multinationals, factories, NGOs, and small enterprises. Systems may differ in scale, but all should meet core principles: Prevention, safe reporting, fair investigation, accountability, and remedy. The Act should establish rights and duties; rules provide the machinery but cannot fill substantive gaps.
Why does this matter?
Workers should be able to speak up without risking livelihood, dignity or safety. For organizations, a fair process can address concerns before they escalate.
Trade unions gain confidence that workers can raise concerns without retaliation; employers’ organizations gain a more consistent playing field. The government can show that its commitments are more than words, while development organizations sustain donor confidence.
For businesses, the issue extends across supply chains. Buyers want evidence that worker voice, grievance mechanisms, and remedies function in practice, not simply that a policy exists.
There is also a market-access dimension. The EU is Bangladesh’s largest trading partner, and textiles are a major part of its imports from Bangladesh.
After LDC graduation, Bangladesh is due to retain Everything But Arms preferences for at least three years under the revised EU GSP framework and may seek GSP+. The framework emphasizes human rights, labour rights, and good governance.
From December 14, 2027, the EU Forced Labour Regulation will prohibit products made with forced labour from being placed on or made available in the EU market. Harassment is not itself forced labour, but violence, intimidation, and abuse of vulnerability can be relevant to wider forced-labour risks. Market access depends on price, quality, and delivery, but also on evidence that labour rights are respected.
This is not simply about compliance; it is about good governance and good business. A credible system protects rights, reduces productivity losses, supports responsible supply chains, gives effect to international commitments, and helps safeguard market access.
“Zero tolerance” should not mean zero complaints. A workplace with no complaints may be safe, or it may be one where people do not feel safe enough to speak. Zero tolerance should mean zero tolerance for harassment, retaliation, and inaction.
Bangladesh has moved towards legal reform. The next step is to make the law and rules work together. That is where the real test of reform will lie.
Jenefa Jabbar is Barrister-at-Law and Principal, JJC. This article has been developed through Bangladesh Institute of Labour Studies- BILS and GoodWeave International under the project titled “Promoting Living Wage, Labour Rights, and Human Rights Due Diligence in Bangladesh.”

item.title: When the state becomes a family business
item.description:
Democracy can persist through elections, legislative bodies, and formal constitutions, yet it can simultaneously erode the essential public dimension of governance. When familial ties, political allegiance, and private wealth dictate access to power and the allocation of public resources, democracy risks devolving into an empty framework encasing a privatized political economy. Bangladesh is not an exception.
“Nepotocracy” extends beyond the mere favouring of relatives by individual politicians; it characterizes a systemic phenomenon where dynastic relationships serve as conduits for the perpetuation of political influence.
Kleptocracy, by contrast, describes a regime in which public authority is systematically exploited for personal financial gain.
In Bangladesh, nepotism and kleptocracy are significantly prominent, diminishing public trust in political parties and the government.
The peril escalates when these two systems reinforce one another. Familial networks can safeguard access to political authority, while wealth accrued through political channels can further entrench and replicate these familial structures.
Consequently, a political-economic feedback loop emerges, in which the distinctions between familial, state, and private capital become increasingly indistinct.
Are elections enough?
Contemporary political discourse frequently positions elections as the cornerstone of democracy. However, elections alone do not ensure democratic governance, especially in countries with limited law enforcement and widespread political fragmentation, such as Bangladesh.
A nation may conduct regular elections, yet political competition can remain profoundly imbalanced. It can boast a constitutional framework while powerful entities operate through informal networks that bypass formal processes.
Parliamentary structures may exist, but legislators often find themselves beholden to party leadership or influential political patrons. The judiciary may exist, yet political influence can compromise its independence.
Thus, the critical concern transcends the mere existence of democratic institutions; it lies in their functional integrity.
The World Bank's political-economy framework provides valuable insights in this regard, telling us how skewed power distributions can foster exclusion, capture, and clientelism, ultimately eroding effective governance, equity, and developmental progress.
This distinction is paramount. Democracy cannot merely be viewed as an assembly of institutional frameworks. It must also be understood as a dynamic system of relationships through which power is allocated and exercised.
When a select political family or interlinked elite networks monopolize these relationships, a veneer of formal democracy can coexist with substantive socio-economic inequality, and we have seen this practice in Bangladesh since its independence in 1971.
From nepotism to nepotocracy
Nepotism is a well-known phenomenon wherein individuals in positions of power extend preferential treatment to family members, close associates, and stakeholders with shared interests.
This practice often aims to optimize wealth accumulation and profits, frequently through questionable or unethical operations. It highlights the implications of familial and social ties in decision-making processes, potentially undermining fairness and meritocracy in both economic and organizational contexts.
While nepotism is rampant in political structures, where familial relationships heavily influence appointments, succession, economic advantages, and access to state resources, nepotocracy is something larger.
There is a difference between isolated instances of favouritism, which may breach public-sector integrity but don't destabilize the political system, and systemic nepotism, where family ties continually affect political parties, government agencies, and institutions, ultimately perpetuating political power.
Does political power begin to acquire a hereditary character?
Yes, familial networks can be important for political success. "Political capital" means the trust and influence a person has in politics. Politicians use it to gain support for their ideas, influence public opinion, or achieve goals.
Family members often build connections over time, allowing them to pass down financial support from one generation to the next. Relationships with government officials, businesses, and media can also boost these advantages.
This dynamic does not necessarily eliminate electoral processes. Instead, elections unfold within a framework in which certain political actors have disproportionately more resources and networks than their counterparts.
This scenario poses a complex democratic challenge: What are the implications when political competition remains formally inclusive, yet access to political authority becomes increasingly concentrated among a limited number of familial dynasties?
Modern nepotocracy in Bangladesh
Sociologist Max Weber provides a valuable framework for understanding authority structures, distinguishing between rational-legal authority and patrimonial authority. In a rational-legal bureaucracy, authority is institutional rather than personal; established rules and qualifications fill positions, and decision-making follows formal protocols.
In the context of Bangladesh, the concepts of patrimonial authority and modern nepotocracy resonate strongly with the political and administrative landscape. The country has a long history of political dynasties in which loyalty to specific leaders or families plays a critical role in governance.
In many cases, political power is less about democratic processes and more about personal connections and kinship ties, which reflects the principles of patrimonial authority.
Governance in Bangladesh is hybrid, blending formal democratic structures with traditional patronage networks. Although the constitution supports democratic principles, political appointments often rely on personal loyalties rather than expertise, leading to ineffective leadership.
This undermines public trust and productivity. Despite grassroots movements advocating change, newly elected administrations often continue their predecessors' autocratic practices, hindering institutional reform and democratic accountability. In public administration, political connections often compromise recruitment despite a facade of merit-based processes.
The state consequently operates according to two competing logics: Formal rational-legal institutions and informal patrimonial networks.
The tension between those two systems is at the heart of the problem in any country, especially in Bangladesh.
When political power becomes economic capital
In Bangladesh, kleptocracy is particularly relevant when examining the intersection of political power and economic resources. The dynamics described earlier can be observed in how political officeholders often prioritize personal enrichment over public welfare.
In Bangladesh, governance challenges are often highlighted by allegations of corruption and mismanagement, in which a select few in power misappropriate public resources.
Political patronage plays a crucial role in distributing government contracts, land, and natural resources. For example, infrastructure projects intended for public benefit often end up bolstering the interests of politically-connected groups, illustrating how public assets are redirected for private gain.
Moreover, the persistent interests that shape state policy in Bangladesh often favour elite networks, reinforcing systemic inequalities.
The contradiction becomes evident as citizens see institutions formally designated as public entities while the economic benefits that should accrue to the broader population increasingly concentrate within a narrow circle of the political elite.
This situation reflects a shift in the allure of political office in Bangladesh -- from a genuine commitment to serve the public good to a pathway for accessing rents and economic opportunities.
Political engagement can indeed resemble a financial investment for many politicians and their affiliates, shifting the focus away from serving constituents and toward maximizing personal or collective financial benefits.
Consequently, this analysis of kleptocracy not only sheds light on the structural vulnerabilities within Bangladesh's political and economic systems but also emphasizes the need for reforms that prioritize accountability and transparency to reclaim public resources for the benefit of all citizens.
The family and the money trail
Nepotism and corruption present serious dangers, particularly when they reinforce each other. Imagine a political system where trusted family members and close associates hold key positions. These positions grant them access to vital information, public contracts, regulatory decisions, and government resources. As a result, economically-influential groups benefit, concentrating private wealth.
This wealth can then be utilized to back political groups, finance electoral campaigns, and maintain patronage systems. Consequently, the political structure becomes increasingly fortified as the cycle continues.
This dynamic can be briefly outlined as follows:
Family political dominance → loyal appointments → institutional takeover → preferential access to public assets → wealth gathering → political funding and patronage → strengthened political connections → further institutional takeover.
Understanding this cyclical pattern is essential to grasp how corruption endures even after individual officials are removed. The problem often goes beyond specific corrupt politicians; it involves an institutional framework that consistently incentivises political actors to repeat such actions.
From bribery to state capture
Over the years, Bangladesh has faced significant challenges related to governance, characterized by various forms of corruption, including bribery and systematic manipulation of state mechanisms.
Bribery often manifests in public services, where officials may accept kickbacks to expedite processes or bypass regulations. This creates an environment where the rule of law is undermined, and ordinary citizens may struggle to access essential services without resorting to illicit practices.
However, the more insidious issue of state capture is particularly relevant to understanding the dynamics of power in Bangladesh.
Prominent political actors have been known to influence the formulation of laws and regulations to benefit their interests or those of their supporters.
For example, the crafting of contracts in infrastructure projects or natural resource extraction can be tailored to favour companies with political ties, often marginalizing competition and compromising fair business practices.
Moreover, the privatization processes in Bangladesh have raised concerns about the transfer of state assets to politically-connected businesses, sometimes disguised as legitimate transactions.
This not only consolidates power among elite factions but also perpetuates economic inequalities, undermining democratic governance and accountability.
As a result, state capture in Bangladesh shows how the exploitation of public resources can occur within a framework that appears legal, creating an illusion of propriety while eroding public trust and stifling economic development.
Understanding this connection can foster a critical examination of the systemic issues at play and encourage reforms aimed at restoring integrity and accountability in governance.
Nepotocracy thus threatens meritocracy, where social connections can overshadow qualifications and competence, leading to disengagement from public institutions and a focus on relationships over productivity.
This shift fosters corruption as a new norm, distorting competitive environments and leading to institutionalized democratic inequality, where political and economic inequalities reinforce each other.
Kleptocracy operates globally, complicating efforts to combat corruption because illicit wealth moves across borders.
While global financial integration can facilitate development, it also hinders national governments in tracking and recovering corruptly obtained assets. Addressing kleptocracy requires international cooperation among states, financial institutions, and civil society.
Recommendations
Nepotocracy and kleptocracy thrive in Bangladesh due to a complex interplay of political vulnerabilities, social dynamics, and cultural norms. Addressing these issues requires strengthening institutions, promoting transparency, and shifting societal attitudes toward corruption and nepotism.
Only through concerted efforts at various levels can substantial progress be made in combating these prevalent systems.
Strengthening democratic institutions is crucial. Enhancing the independence and capacity of bodies like the judiciary and electoral commissions can help uphold the rule of law free from political interference. Promote transparency and accountability by establishing mechanisms for public access to government contracts and financial disclosures, supported by independent audits of public spending.
Encouraging civic engagement is another vital component. Fostering an active civil society and public awareness campaigns can empower citizens to participate in governance and hold their leaders accountable.
Additionally, implementing anti-nepotism laws with clear guidelines will help ensure that merit prevails over familial connections in public appointments.
Political reforms should aim to democratize party structures and introduce term limits to reduce the concentration of elite power. Lastly, enhancing economic opportunities for all, regardless of family ties, will help create a more equitable society.
By addressing these interrelated issues, Bangladesh can pave the way for genuine democratic governance that prioritizes the common good and fosters sustainable development.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.

item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) opened its January spectrum auction, expecting the high-stakes competition typical of vital national infrastructure sales. Instead, the room fell silent.
Grameenphone acquired 10 MHz of the 700 MHz band at the base reserve price of Tk 2,370 crore, Robi withdrew, while Banglalink stayed away from the bidding, leaving 10 MHz of the unsold spectrum to be assigned later to state-owned Teletalk at the same rate.
Failing to attract competition, this transaction left policy-makers with a critical question: How can such an auction dictate the pricing of an upcoming renewal cycle?
The short answer is it cannot . True market value requires viable alternatives where operators bid for expansion, not survival. Spectrum renewal offers no such luxury.
Once a mobile operator anchors its network architecture around a specific band and deploys thousands of base stations, walking away is no longer an option. A renewal price has little to do with market value; it is apparently a reflection of short-term state treasury demands colliding with an operator's inability to walk away without shutting down their business.
This structural disconnect matters as Bangladesh approaches the November renewal of spectrum in the 900 MHz, 1.8 GHz, and 2.1 GHz bands. Data from the GSMA’s 2025 study reveals that Bangladesh’s spectrum costs consume 15.7% of operators’ recurring revenues, much higher than the Asia-Pacific median of 10.4% and the global median of 7.7%.
Macroeconomic modeling suggests that cutting this economic burden to half could unlock $34 billion in cumulative economic benefits by 2035 and a 75% reduction could generate $45bn. These numbers are no prescription to slash prices; rather, they must be weighed against the state’s undeniable fiscal duty to manage a public asset.
At the same time, operators need capital for advanced radios and network upgrades. The real policy challenge is not finding an arbitrary, magic price per megahertz, but ensuring that every megahertz becomes highly productive.
Spectrum productivity is best measured by its capacity for dense urban hubs, wider coverage for rural villages, and reliable network quality during peak hours. Yet, BTRC data exposes a deep structural imbalance in our airwaves.
State-owned Teletalk holds 65.2 MHz for just 6.8 million subscribers, while Grameenphone must squeeze 84.4 million subscribers into 137.4 MHz. Serving remote terrain explains part of this gap, but not all of it.
When rigid frameworks lock spectrum in underutilized silos while urban networks suffer from congestion, the scarcity becomes artificial. Because traffic patterns shift constantly, a band that was adequate five years ago may leave one city congested today while sitting idle in another. If frequency blocks cannot move dynamically to match this shifting public demand, the consumer experience inevitably degrades, and the broader digital economy suffers.
Other nations have long recognized that draining an operator's capital through high upfront spectrum fees may starve the investments needed for network rollouts. Many have shifted toward models that trade immediate financial burdens for guaranteed socio-economic outcomes.
India addressed artificial scarcity by legalizing spectrum trading and sharing , allowing rights to move toward operators facing heavy traffic. Its framework permitted transfers subject to spectrum caps, roll-out obligations, eligibility conditions and a two-year holding period, with a 1% transfer fee.
Similarly, Austria and Colombia tied their low-band spectrum licensing directly to rural coverage, allowing operators to earn explicit fee discounts or convert coverage commitments into cash-equivalent credits. Spain and Canada chose to extend license terms or waive upfront renewal fees where operators could demonstrate minimum population coverage , giving companies the necessary breathing room to amortize massive hardware investments.
The warnings from the global markets should also be watched closely. In its multi-band auction, Pakistan cut reserve prices on legacy bands by more than 50%, yet those bands still drew no bids.
This proved that artificial benchmarks fail to create demand for spectrum that lacks commercial viability. In contrast, Vietnam demonstrates the power of flexible strategic asset pricing; after a failed 2023 auction, it slashed reserve prices by nearly 80%, separating long-term economic utility from the temptation of short-term cash extraction to rapidly achieve roughly 90% 5G coverage by early 2026.
Meanwhile, other regulatory experiments show distinct operational challenges: Austria faced ambiguity over how coverage would be measured. Colombia’s process was criticized for hiding minimum bids in advance while miscalculating rural rollout costs.
Finally, Canada’s model serves as a direct warning; its rigid obligation conditions drove up holding costs without incentivizing efficient use, creating long-term operational inefficiencies after the regulator ignored industry challenges during consultations.
To break out of the cycle of revenue-maximizing deadlocks and deteriorating network quality, Bangladesh needs a pragmatic, forward-looking approach. Rather than exhausting operator liquidity through high upfront hurdles, BTRC can incentivize infrastructure development by recalibrating its renewal fees into a more manageable, back-loaded payment timeline.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad is a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy. He is shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org .

item.description:
We have made our micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) the egg-laying, wool-bearing, milk-giving pig -- the German fantasy animal that does everything at once.
We want them to give jobs to men, women, and people with disabilities. We want them to go green, though the market pays no premium for going green. We want them to sell at the lowest price while their rent, raw materials, and transport costs all rise. We want them to transact with the bank, pay taxes.
Then we complain that the MSMEs are informal. But we fail to address the concern that formality raises production costs while the shelf price stays the same.
We bring them to seminars. We pat their backs. We give them awards. And every seminar opens with the same sentence: MSMEs do not have access to credit. And that cycle goes on for decades. We leave the ground hostile yet ask these small firms to carry the country to a trillion dollars.
We must be living in a fool’s paradise.
The situation however could be improved and MSMEs can indeed be a conduit to the trillion dollars hope.
But the MSMEs will not be able to do it alone. They can do it if we see MSMEs and large businesses as a nexus and in the same value creation network.
A food safety certification costs the same whether you sell to one shop or five hundred. So does a cold chain, a compliance officer, a brand, a gas connection, a distribution network. These are fixed costs.
A large firm spreads them across enormous volumes while a firm turning over Tk50 lakh a year cannot spread them at all. So when a cost shock arrives, it does not land equally. It irritates the large firm. It kills the small one.
That is the story of the last 11 years. The charts tell it.
Sources: BBS price indices; Energy Division fuel notifications; BERC orders; Bangladesh Bank. Marketing and gas are charted on a separate scale. Values for 2026 are estimates; dashed segments are projected.
Since 2015, rent has risen 93%. That is the CPI housing group, since Bangladesh publishes no commercial rent index. Producer prices for raw materials are up 64%, diesel 63%, electricity for business premises 61%. Industrial gas has risen more than five times. Marketing has risen more than nine times.
Now reflect: How much has the price gone up on the bag you bought last month from a boutique on Facebook? Zero, or close to it.
Look at how fast it arrived. Diesel rose 42.5% in a single night on August 6, 2022. Gas for large industries rose 150% in one order on February 1, 2023, from about Tk 11 to Tk 28 per cubic metre.
The retail electricity tariff rose again on June 1, 2026, and the small-industry tariff rose 18.3% against a system average of 16.7%. The small firm was charged above the average.
Source: Energy and Mineral Resources Division and BPC price notifications, 2015–2026, verified against reporting in Dhaka Tribune, The Daily Star, Prothom Alo, The Business Standard.
Sources: BERC gas tariff orders, 2017–2025, and BERC and Power Division electricity tariff orders, 2015–2026.
One number deserves far more attention. Industrial gas costs Tk 30 per cubic metre for an existing user. For a new user it costs Tk 40. We charge the entrant a third more than the incumbent. We say we want new firms to emerge and inefficient ones to make way. Then we put a price on entry.
Marketing tells the same story. In 2015 it cost Tk 30 to reach a thousand people on Facebook. By 2022 it was Tk 98. Today it is Tk 280.
Roughly Tk 65 of that is Bangladeshi VAT and withholding tax. Much of the rest is the fall of the taka. Only a fraction is Meta raising its price.
Since Covid-19, hundreds of thousands of MSMEs built their businesses on f-commerce. Their cost of finding a customer has risen ninefold while the price they charge has barely moved.
Sources: LightCastle Partners, Digital Marketing Landscape Bangladesh 2015; agency benchmark studies, 2022 and 2026; Bangladesh Bank FE Circular No. 04 of 8 May 2023.
So where has the money gone? The consumer pays far more than she did a decade ago. The producer does not receive it. What sits between them has widened: Transport, storage, spoilage, tolls, layer upon layer of trading, and the VAT and duty increases of January 2025.
When we discuss inflation, we take the side of the consumers; but barely we think of the producers who are also choking to death. The producer and the buyer are not opponents. They are two ends of the same rope.
This is why consumers should worry about the small firm. As MSMEs thin out, the cheapest supply goes first. The neighbourhood producer, the small trader, the one-room manufacturer who kept the price honest.
Fewer sellers mean less competition, and less competition means the consumer pays more.
I was sitting recently with the chief executive of one of our largest agro-logistics companies. He was explaining their struggle to source and sell rural produce in their urban outlets.
The cold storage network in Bangladesh is old and was built for potatoes; so the company cannot use it for perishables. Despite the investment in highways, congestion remains.
Recently they tried an innovative scheme to source fresh sweet from the South and sell it in outlets in Dhaka. Half the fresh-milk sweets became stale on arrival.
I can write a book on my experience in trying to solve these supply chain challenges. I remember in 2010, we wanted to promote crates to cut post-harvest losses on pineapple shipped from the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
The crown took up nearly half the cargo space and bruised half the load. And when the load spoiled, the trader pushed the loss down to the small farmer.
In a chain without contracts, loss flows downhill until it reaches whoever has the least power to refuse it.
It does not have to work that way though. Between roughly 2006 and 2016, large numbers of cattle were distributed to char dwellers in the northern districts. It soon became clear there was no high-yielding fodder.
The next round of interventions built the fodder system and then the artificial insemination system. Later, the sheer volume of cattle resulted in processing capacity. A system formed.
But notice how it formed. One missing piece at a time, over a decade. It became a system only when a large buyer appeared at the end of it.
That is what Bangladesh is missing. Our policy imagines large and small enterprises as rivals. It treats the corporate sector as something the MSME must be shielded from, and the MSME as something to be supported separately: Its own ministry, its own foundation, its own seminar.
The two never meet. The small firm faces the market alone. It buys at the worst price in the chain, sells at the worst price in the chain, and absorbs every shock that is passed down.
Bangladesh does not need thousands of grocery shops each bargaining alone against a fragmented wholesale market. It needs them inside networks.
This is the road our neighbours took, and they did not leave it to chance.
In Vietnam, the Ministry of Industry and Trade partnered with Samsung to build a domestic supplier base, sending engineers into Vietnamese factories to bring them up to standard.
More than 300 Vietnamese firms now sit in Samsung's supplier tiers. Malaysia has run a Vendor Development Program for decades, registering anchor companies, matching them with small vendors and financing those vendors through a dedicated bank window.
In Thailand, more than 10,000 7-Eleven outlets trade. Most are franchised to individual owner-operators who buy through one system rather than a hundred.
In Indonesia and the Philippines, millions of warungs and sari-sari stores are the exact counterparts of our mudir dokan . Supply platforms now give these one-room shops something close to the buying price of a chain.
In none of these countries did the small shop close. It stopped standing alone, and networked small firms carried those economies upward.
How can we fix this?
The MSMEs in Bangladesh will deliver the trillion-dollar economy. But they cannot deliver it in the arrangement we have built for them: A few million firms, each operating alone, each absorbing every shock the system passes down, each competing against the large enterprise that ought to be its customer.
However, if we put the small and the large enterprises in the common nexus of creating value, the trillion-dollar hope will arrive soon.

Can we ever have safer roads?
item.description:
That the Road Safety Foundation reported that at least 438 lives were lost in crashes across Bangladesh in June alone no longer surprises us, nor elicits any strong response. This is what we have been reduced to, when hundreds of lives lost every month have become so commonplace that the nation collectively barely registers it.
Behind each number lies a family shattered and a community scarred. But most of all, every month, we are reminded that as a nation, we continue to fail to protect citizens on the roads.
The causes are painfully familiar: Reckless driving, unfit vehicles, weak enforcement, and poor infrastructure. Year after year, probes are announced, awareness campaigns launched, and promises made.
Yet the death toll never budges. Road safety in Bangladesh has long been a crisis, yet we seem to be drifting further away from doing something about it.
Despite the public marching in 2018, and despite numerous calls for overhaul, what we continue to lack is structural reform. There remains woeful licensing standards, no mandatory vehicle fitness checks, and no effort to ensure genuine enforcement of traffic laws.
All of this points back to our culture of impunity. Too often, powerful transport owners and reckless drivers escape accountability, undermining justice. Road safety cannot improve until violations carry real consequences.
Bangladesh’s roads should not be death traps, yet they continue to be. Every life lost is a reminder that safety should not be optional but a right for every person in this country.

item.title: Preparing for the inevitable
item.description:
That Bangladesh is likely to face flooding in July and August, according to forecasts, should not be a surprise. We have long known that our geography and climate, in addition to the adverse effect of climate change, make floods inevitable for our nation.
What remains surprising, and unacceptable, is how often we remain unprepared despite knowing what is coming.
Floods, beyond being natural events, have long been a test for our governance. Each year, families lose homes, crops are destroyed, and livelihoods are disrupted.
Each year, relief arrives, but too late and too little. The cycle of damage and recovery continues, while prevention and preparedness remain neglected.
Suffice to say, this is not a solution.
Preparedness must begin before the waters rise. From strengthening embankments to clearing drainage systems to ensuring shelters are stocked and accessible. From mobilizing local authorities to identify vulnerable communities to coordinating evacuation plans.
In addition, we must also ensure that relief funds are transparent and reach those who need them most, rather than being lost to corruption or inefficiency.
Technology and data must also play a crucial role. Early warning systems must be expanded and communicated effectively, not buried in bureaucratic channels.
Simultaneously, we need more investment in resilient infrastructure across the country, from roads, schools, and hospitals, where they are needed most, not where the most headlines are generated.
Bangladesh has lived with floods for centuries, but living with them should not mean suffering from them. Preparedness is cheaper than recovery, and prevention saves lives. The government must treat the coming floods not as an annual inconvenience but as a national priority.

item.title: Receiving our fair share from the carbon market
item.description:
The government's decision to strengthen Bangladesh's carbon market marks an encouraging step towards aligning economic development with environmental responsibility.
As climate change continues to intensify, countries must look beyond conventional environmental policies and embrace market-based mechanisms that reward sustainable practices, while discouraging excessive emissions.
For a climate-vulnerable nation like Bangladesh, such initiatives are not merely desirable but increasingly necessary: A well-functioning carbon market can attract investment, encourage cleaner technologies, and provide businesses with incentives to reduce their carbon footprint.
It also has the potential to unlock new sources of climate finance, helping fund renewable energy, conservation projects, and other low-carbon initiatives.
If implemented effectively, it could strengthen Bangladesh's position in global climate negotiations while contributing to long-term economic resilience.
However, ambitious announcements alone will not deliver meaningful results. Clear regulations, transparent monitoring, and strong institutional capacity will be integral to building a credible carbon market.
Emissions data must be accurate and independently verified, while enforcement mechanisms should ensure that participants comply with established standards.
Policymakers must also engage industries, financial institutions, and environmental experts throughout the process to design a practical and trusted system.
It is also important to ensure that the carbon market complements broader climate action. Expanding renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, protecting forests and wetlands, promoting sustainable transport, and encouraging climate-smart agriculture must remain central pillars of national policy.
Public awareness will also be crucial, as businesses and citizens alike need to understand both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with a low-carbon economy.
Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its commitment to addressing climate challenges, despite contributing only a small share of global emissions. Strengthening the carbon market reflects that commitment and deserves recognition.
We must now translate this intent into action -- through consistent policies, effective implementation, and unwavering political will.
The success of this decision will depend on the discipline we display to see it through.

item.title: Building a modern public transport system
item.description:
That Dhaka’s metro rail will begin operating up to Kamalapur in April 2027 is certainly welcome news.
Once completed, the extension will connect the capital’s busiest railway station with the country’s first metro line, making travel faster, more convenient, and better integrated for countless commuters.
This is another important step towards building a modern urban transport system that Dhaka has desperately needed for decades. Test runs are expected to begin in January, with work on the extension now well advanced.
The real challenge now, however, is in ensuring that the project reaches the finish line exactly as promised.
Bangladesh has seen too many infrastructure projects suffer from repeated deadline extensions, escalating costs, and unnecessary administrative delays, and the Kamalapur extension must not become another example of that.
Authorities should maintain strict oversight, ensure transparency in procurement and implementation, and resolve any remaining technical issues without compromising quality or safety.
Delivering the project on schedule and within budget would strengthen public confidence and demonstrate that major infrastructure can, indeed, be completed efficiently.
At the same time, this extension should not be viewed as the end goal; Dhaka's growing population and worsening traffic congestion demand a far broader transformation of public transportation.
The metro rail alone cannot solve the city's mobility crisis: Other planned MRT lines, bus rapid transit systems, commuter rail improvements, and better integration between buses, trains, and metro services must all move forward without losing momentum.
At the same time, reliable pedestrian access and affordable fares must be prioritized for more people to embrace public transport over private vehicles.
While the progress towards Kamalapur deserves recognition, it should also reinforce the urgency of completing the wider vision.
Bangladesh must continue investing in efficient, accessible, and sustainable public transportation -- because the economic, environmental, and social benefits will far outweigh the costs for generations to come.
